question.text: For a moving coil galvanometer, the deflection in the coil is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>05</mn><mo> </mo><mi>rad</mi></math> when a current of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>10</mn><mo> </mo><mi>mA</mi></math> is passed through it. If the torsional constant of suspension wire is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>0</mn><mo> </mo><mo>×</mo><mo> </mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>–</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi>rad</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>, the magnetic field is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>01</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></math> and the number of turns in the coil is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>200</mn></math>, the area of each turn (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>cm</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> ) is :

solution.text:
Given: θ=0.05 rad, I=10 mA, K=4×10-5 N m rad-1, B=0.01 T, N=200

The torsional constant of a wire used in a moving coil galvanometer is given by 

K=NIABθ, where, A is area of each turn

So, A=KθNIB=4×10-5×0.05200×10×10-3×0.01

Thus, A=10-4 m2=1 cm2
